newsitem.title: UK: BRITISH OLYMPIC CHIEFS BACK SPORTS ACADEMY SCHEME.
newsitem.headline: BRITISH OLYMPIC CHIEFS BACK SPORTS ACADEMY SCHEME.

text.p: British Olympic chiefs, worried by the country's dwindling sporting status, on Monday announced their backing for a 175-million-pound ($286-million) plan for a national sports academy in Heyford, central England.
British Olympic Association chairman Craig Reedie, pledged an annual one million pounds ($1.64 million) funding for the academy if it is built in Heyford.

The Heyford proposal is one of 25 bids recieved by the government and involves transforming part of an old United States Air Force base into a centre catering for sports including table tennis, rugby, sprinting and volleyball.

Launching the bid at a news conference, former British foreign secretary Douglas Hurd, who represents the Heyford area in parliament, said: "Sport is, or should be, one of Britain's major assets in the world."

But in an apparent reference to this year's Olympic Games in Atlanta, where Britons won just one gold medal, he added: "We have not been doing as well as we should. We need to look at that and find ways to remedy it."
Prime Minister John Major, a keen football and cricket fan, has already promised up to 100 million pounds ($164 million) of funding from Britain's National Lottery for an academy of sport.
But the Heyford bid has an additional 75 million pounds ($122.8 million) in private sector backing, largely from building firms which plan to develop other areas of the old base for housing.

Reedie said it could ensure "that every sportsman and sportswoman who has the capacity to excel at international level will enjoy the highest standards of coaching, sports medicine and sports science".
